title: Sell Mineral Rights in Colorado
metaTitle: Sell Mineral Rights in Colorado | DJ, Piceance
metaDescription: Weld County DJ basin oil check or western slope Piceance gas royalty? Colorado plays behave differently. Get a fair offer built off your actual statements.
heroLead: Where your Colorado check comes from matters more than almost anywhere else, an active Weld County oil well and a legacy Piceance gas well are two completely different situations.
intro: Colorado splits pretty cleanly into two mineral-owning experiences. Around Greeley and across Weld County, the Denver-Julesburg basin is still an active horizontal drilling area, oil-heavy with associated gas, and operators there continue permitting new units, particularly on the fringes of existing development. If your check comes from that part of the state, you may still see real upside from infill drilling.

Out on the western slope, the Piceance basin around Garfield and Rio Blanco counties is a different story, a mature, mostly dry-gas field that was drilled hard in the 2000s and has seen very little new activity since gas prices pulled back. Owners there are almost always looking at a slow, steady decline with little chance of a new well changing that.

sections.heading: DJ Basin Owners: Watch for New Unit Activity
paragraphs: Weld County is one of the few places in the country where operators are still actively permitting new horizontal wells, so a DJ basin interest carries a different kind of uncertainty than a legacy field. Your existing well may be declining normally while a new unit gets permitted next door that could bring your interest back up in a year or two.

That upside cuts both ways when you are deciding whether to sell. An offer on active DJ basin acreage typically accounts for both the current well's decline and any known permitted activity nearby, since that is real information available through the state's oil and gas commission filings.

sections.heading: Piceance Basin Checks Are a Different Read
paragraphs: If your statement shows a well operating in Garfield, Rio Blanco, or Mesa County with gas-only production, you are most likely in the Piceance, and the honest read is that new drilling there has been minimal for years. These are mature gas wells declining on a predictable curve with essentially no drilling program behind them right now.

Deductions on Piceance gas checks often run heavier than on an oil check because of the gathering and processing infrastructure required to move gas out of that part of the state, so a lower net number relative to gross volume is normal here, not a red flag.

sections.heading: Colorado's Regulatory Environment Shapes Both Plays
paragraphs: Colorado has tightened setback and permitting rules over the past several years, particularly around populated areas of Weld County. That has slowed, but not stopped, new DJ basin permitting, and it is worth knowing that regulatory friction is part of why some units take longer to get drilled than they used to.

For Piceance owners, regulation is less of a factor than simple economics, dry gas in a remote part of the state competing against cheaper gas basins elsewhere. Either way, it is useful context when you are trying to understand why your check moves the way it does.

sections.heading: Getting an Offer on Either Type of Interest
paragraphs: Send your most recent statements and we will identify which basin and county your interest sits in from the operator name and well information. DJ basin offers factor in nearby permitted activity where it exists; Piceance offers are built almost entirely off documented decline, since new drilling is not a realistic near-term factor there.

From there, closing runs through a standard mineral deed and a title check at the county clerk's office where the interest is recorded, usually Weld County for DJ basin interests or Garfield, Rio Blanco, or Mesa County for Piceance interests. Most closings wrap up within a few weeks once ownership and any co-owner details are confirmed.

faqs.question: Is there still active drilling in the DJ basin?
faqs.answer: Yes, particularly in Weld County, where operators continue permitting new horizontal wells, though setback rules and local approvals have slowed the pace compared to the 2010s peak.

faqs.question: Why is your Piceance basin gas check smaller than you expected?
faqs.answer: Gathering and processing costs for gas moving out of the Piceance tend to run higher than for oil production elsewhere, which shows up as larger deductions between the gross production volume and your net royalty.

faqs.question: Should you wait to sell if your well is in an active drilling area?
faqs.answer: That depends on your own timeline and risk tolerance. Active areas carry real upside potential from new units, but also carry the uncertainty of permitting delays, so we walk through what is currently filed near your interest before you decide.

faqs.question: How do you know which basin your Colorado interest is in?
faqs.answer: The operator name and well or unit information on your statement will tell us. Weld County interests are almost always DJ basin; Garfield, Rio Blanco, or Mesa County interests are almost always Piceance.

faqs.question: Do Colorado's setback rules affect the value of your interest?
faqs.answer: They can, mainly by slowing how quickly nearby permits move from filing to drilling. It is a factor we consider for DJ basin acreage specifically, since it affects how much weight nearby permitted activity should carry in an offer.
